instruction_text: Swap white rice for basmati rice — its lower GI (54 vs 73) meaningfully reduces the glycemic load of this meal.
reason: Basmati rice has a substantially lower GI than common milled white rice due to its longer grain and higher amylose content.

instruction_text: Swap maida bhature for missi roti (besan + atta blend) — much lower GI and higher protein and fiber.
reason: Missi roti made from a chickpea flour and whole wheat blend has a GI around 28 vs maida's 76, and adds protein and fiber.

instruction_text: Use 1 tsp of ghee instead of 2–3 tsp when finishing the dish — the flavour carries at lower quantity.
reason: Ghee is predominantly saturated fat (62g/100g); small reductions meaningfully lower meal-level saturated fat.

instruction_text: Replace coconut oil with mustard oil — mustard oil has a much better unsaturated fat profile for heart health.
reason: Coconut oil is ~83% saturated fat; mustard oil is ~12% saturated fat with a high MUFA:SFA ratio.

instruction_text: Reduce ghee quantity — its low MUFA:SFA ratio is the main driver of the fat quality score. Use 1 tsp instead of 2.
reason: Ghee has a MUFA:SFA ratio well below 0.5, pushing the meal into the lowest fat quality band.

instruction_text: Replace refined sunflower oil with mustard oil — mustard oil has a higher MUFA:SFA ratio and is the traditional South Asian cooking oil.
reason: Sunflower oil is predominantly PUFA with moderate MUFA; mustard oil has a higher MUFA content and is the MASALA SAM score reference fat.

instruction_text: Replace cream with curd (yogurt) in the gravy — similar creamy texture, much lower saturated fat.
reason: Heavy cream is ~23g saturated fat per 100g; full-fat curd is ~2g per 100g, with added probiotic benefit.

instruction_text: Add a vegetable side (spinach, methi, or bhindi) to boost fiber. This meal is low in fiber.
reason: Fiber is independently protective for both T2D and CVD; non-starchy green vegetables are the lowest-calorie way to add fiber to a South Asian meal.

instruction_text: Add a small portion of moong dal or masoor dal — legume protein is independently protective for both diabetes and heart disease risk in South Asian populations.
reason: ICMR-INDIAB found legume and dairy protein independently associated with lower T2D risk; replacing 5% of carbohydrate energy with plant protein was significantly protective.
